utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84bis-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj, Idriz Balaj, and Lahi Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Daniela Kravetz, appearing for the Prosecution, together with my colleague, Aditya Menon, and our case manager, Line Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Kravetz. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Ben Emmerson for Ramush Haradinaj, together with Rod Dixon, Annie O'Reilly, and Andrew Strong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Gregor Guy-Smith, with Holly Buchanan, Colleen Rohan, and Mr. Zyberi remains with us. And could I take this moment also to ask for some assistance from the technical service at this moment because one of my computers is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can help him with that, Madam Registrar. And for Mr. Brahimaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Richard Harvey, assisted by Mr. Paul Troop, Ms. Sophie Rigney, Ms. -- ouch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Assisted by Ms. Ouch?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sorry, my microphone started an interesting gyration. Rudina Jasini and Mr. Luke Boenisch. Thank you, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Good morning. I have very few questions left for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could please have up on the screen 03071. And if the Serbian version could be displayed for the witness, and if we could have the English and the original for the rest of the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the Serbian version of this document before you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I have a few questions about this document and we'll just start from the top. We see it starts by saying: "To Smajl in Gllogjan - from Gani." And it's signed 30th May 1998, Tropoja, Gani. First, sir, do you know who this person referred to is, Smajl in Gllogjan, is, who this reference refers to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us who that is.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a pseudonym used by Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we see at the bottom it says "Tropoja." Could you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a small town in northern Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to read a portion of the document to you. It says: "Smajl, we are aware of the situation in Kosovo. The problem here is that we have none of the things that people need. "The problem is that a lot of people have come to us, almost all with your signature, and the problem is that prices have risen a lot for these people who are buying Kalashnikovs themselves," and indicates the types of weapons. And if we go down a couple of lines, it says: "I would like to ask you as a friend to stop sending us people in this way, because we cannot manage to feed them, let alone provide them with resources." Sir, we see this document is referring to a large number of people going to this person in Tropoja with the signature of the person that's being referred to as Smajl, which you've told us is Ramush Haradinaj, to procure weapons. Is the information contained in this document consistent with the information your service had at the time on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I rise with regard to the manner in which the question is asked, specifically the use of the word "consistent," consistent with regard to the question asked has no relevancy. Consistent with what? And what the import of consistent? It comes from nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I can ask it in a different way if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tell us consistent with what, but if you want to ask him, you can ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, I'll see if the witness can respond to the question in the manner it's been put to him, and if not, I'll explore that further.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, could you respond to my question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us what was the source of your information at the time with regard to people going to Albania to procure weapons with documents bearing the signature of Mr. Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a number of sources indicating this. Some of them were the border guard units of the Army of Yugoslavia, they reported about the mass crossings of the border by large groups from Kosovo going to northern Albania and returning and bringing weapons in. And these border control units in that period carried out a series of actions, arresting and liquidating those groups. Other sources were our informants who reported back to us about the activities, about the KLA arming, for example, if you permit me to continue. In late March/early April there were activities by the KLA in the rural area, according to the territorial principle, meaning that practically every village formed a KLA group and one of their primary tasks was to obtain weapons for their activities. So in direct communication and co-operation with the KLA staff in Glodjane, these people, with the knowledge of a part of the KLA leadership in that region of Glodjane, crossed into Albania, purchased weapons, and returned on the same route.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just a clarification on that answer -- regarding that answer, you referred to the period of late March/April -- early April. Which year were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Late March/early April 1998, after the conflict in Glodjane which occurred on the 24th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just clarify some point here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript says at page 5, line -- let me just -- hold it. Page 5, line 5, it says: "With the knowledge of a part of the KLA leadership ..." Is that what the witness said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which part? Which part of the leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The leadership of the group that was acting in the area of the KLA, first of all, Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Anybody else in that -- as part of that leadership? Ramush Haradinaj and who else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His closest associates at the time were Fadil Nimani called Tiger, who was later heading the military police; members of the Mehmetaj family; members of the Shalja family from Dubovik, this was one of the first groups that came to that area and brought weapons to Kosovo from northern Albania. Then there was a logistics centre in Albania headed by members of the KLA, and that is the area where they obtained their weapons and other equipment for their activities in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to know the part that had the knowledge of their activities. Thank you so much. You may proceed, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just very briefly going back to the document, you spoke generally about the leadership in Glodjane and their role. I was speaking about the fact -- the information in this document asking you about the information you had in relation to persons going with the signature of Ramush Haradinaj and crossing into Albania to procure weapons. Did you have information on that specific point; and if yes, could you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early stages, we didn't have too much information about the manner of them going to northern Albania. What we did know was that there were couriers, guides, who transferred groups of people through corridors at the border between Yugoslavia and Albania and then would bring them back. Later in time we received information about how the leaders of those groups had some documents with them which identified them as legitimate representatives of the villages that were going there to obtain arms and equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were you able to obtain this information, that the leaders were -- had some documents which identified them as legitimate representatives of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security centre in Pristina had information that Xheladin Gashi from Glogovac was staying in northern Albania representing one of the persons who was waiting for those groups and making it possible for them to rest, to obtain arms and equipment, and then to return. Also through our intelligence data we knew that Xhavit Haliti was in Albania, his nickname was Zeka, who was the main logistics man of the KLA at the time. This was the information available to us at the time. There was -- there were a number of so-called camps in northern Albania where these villagers from Metohija would arrive, these were villages around Decani, Pec, and Djakovica, and they would go there in order to obtain weapons and equipment. In the early stages, the weapons were distributed for free, but then in time it grew into a business and profit was generated, and all the things happened that usually happened when we're talking about large quantities of money and also due to the fact that more and more people were interested in obtaining weapons --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, can I --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I also know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. I'm just going back to the document. Based on the information you were able to obtain, can you or not confirm that the information in the document we're looking at was correct, and I'm referring specifically to the fact that people were going with documents bearing the signature of Ramush Haradinaj to procure weapons? Can you confirm that the information in the document before you on this matter is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I really couldn't say that at that time, in May 1998, we had information that Ramush Haradinaj was signing certain documents on the basis of which these people would go to obtain weapons. What we did know was that they were not able to go to Albania without the knowledge of Ramush Haradinaj and the group that he led in Glodjane, because Glodjane was on the way to Albania. So it was almost like a check-point through which everyone had to pass on their way to Albania and on the way back from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we show the witness the original version of this document. I know the -- only the Serbian version is being displayed on his screen. Maybe we could have it up on the screen also in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, we see that this document is a handwritten document, the one we've been discussing. During your time with the RDB, have you had the chance to come across or review documents of this type?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I did have the opportunity to see documents like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For the first time, I'm going to ask you to expand a little bit on your answer. If you could explain when you had that opportunity and when these documents came into the possession of your office.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bulk of documents of this kind that we obtained came from the June-September period in 1998, when the police, together with the army, carried out a broader anti-terrorist organisation to unblock roads and break-up KLA strongholds in that area. During that period, when the KLA groups were withdrawing from the areas, we found numerous documents in places where they were billeted. We found equipment, diaries, and all of these things that they left behind when they were withdrawing. So there were many of these documents, documents of this type; there were diaries that some KLA members staying in this area wrote; there were lists of members of the KLA, including the guard posts where they carried out their duties, the people who manned those guard posts; there was equipment; there were uniforms. We even found on the 24th of March, for example, after the Glodjane conflict, we found in the compound of the Haradinaj family, among other documents, lists of Albanians who were suspected of co-operating with members of the Serbian security forces. There were a lot of documents of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to pick up on that answer, can you explain what these lists were that you referred to of Albanians who were suspected of co-operating with members of Serbian security forces? How did you know that these were lists of Albanians suspected of collaborating with members of the security forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just recall a document that we obtained. This was a report sent by Hidajet Hysini [Realtime transcript read in error, Hidajit Hiseni"] then a member of the Presidency of Democratic Alliance of Kosovo, who, for a number of years, was in prison, a member of the national movement for the liberation of Kosovo, who sent it to an unidentified person with suspicions that two women, to two unidentified women, from the Zukaj and Coraj [phoen] families - I'm not quite sure about the families, I think it was the Zukaj and Coraj families - were in contact with the State Security Service of Serbia and that the Serbian security service was gathering information through them about KLA activities. We also obtained a document that indicated that Rasim Sulejmani was involved in activities to gather data information in that period about persons who in any way had contacts with the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just to clarify your answer, you referred to a list of Albanians suspected of collaborating, and then you referred to two families, Zukaj and Coraj families. Were these families or members of those families on the list that you were able to obtain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two women who allegedly had an intimate relationship with one of the members of the security service and that they were gathering information about the KLA activities in that area. If you permit me, I see in the transcript here where it says "Hidajit Hiseni." It's not "Hidajit" but "Hidajet Hysini."

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay, so if I understand your answer correctly, the persons who you have mentioned are persons who were, according to your sources, involved in gathering this information for the KLA. They were not persons who were listed on this list that you saw. Is that a correct understanding, and please correct me if that's not correct or accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you didn't understand me quite correctly. Perhaps I misspoke. It was two women from the families that I referred to. According to Hidajet Hiseni's information were the source of the information for the Serbian security forces. It was the suspicion and information from Hidajet Hiseni. It was something that came from a written document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If I can just maybe word my question differently. What I'm trying to understand is how -- when you saw these lists, how did you know that these were lists of Albanians suspected of collaborating with members of the security forces?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comparing that with our registers of our collaborators network, network of informers, we established that a number of persons were identified as sources of information for the Serbian security service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Now I think the answer is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the document that I was referring to earlier, 03071.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03071 will be Exhibit P127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have one last matter, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And if we could bring up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may go back to the last question that counsel asked. As I understand your answer, there was a -- the information that you had about persons who were sources of information and the -- and your answer to the earlier question which counsel was seeking to ask clarification, as to how it was that you were able to conclude that the lists seized were of persons who were regarded by the KLA, their supporters, as collaborating with the Serbs. I'm not clear as to how it was that you determined that although there was a correspondence or commonality between your lists and theirs, how was it that you determined that the lists that was seized were in terms of how those lists were compiled as lists of collaborators. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. With all due respect, I try to be as brief as possible. The lists had explanations. For example, one of those unidentified women that I mentioned on such and such a day went to the Hotel Pastrik in Djakovica with a state security inspector. I don't want to mention his name. If you insist I can, though. Then Murat Haxhocaj was on that list as well. He is from the village of Luke, I think, and this person was later killed. So next to each name on the list there was an explanation of where, when, and whom they saw. So when you put that against our registers of our informant network, we established and came to the conclusion that these were, we felt, such lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, just to follow-up from that answer, you said that Murat Haxhocaj [Realtime transcript read in error "Haxhozaj"] - it's written on the transcript - was one such person that was listed and was on the list and was later killed. Do you know anything about the circumstances of his death?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, his name is Haxhocaj, I think; in other words, the letter C instead of the letter Z. With all due respect, it's been a long time, but I believe that a group of KLA members took that person out of his family house. I believe that he was staying at the house of a close relative, actually, and that his son was with him as well and that they killed him after that. That's -- I'm now speaking from memory. I know that he was taken out of the house of a close relative by some KLA members and killed later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it's been a long time and I'm asking you a lot of details. Only if you recall, do you know where this person was from, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the event happened at Gornja Luka or Donja Luka. These are villages in the Decani municipality, right next to Decanska Bistrica, not far from Decani itself. It's either Donja Luka or Gornja Luka. These are two villages that are very close to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to clarify, could you tell us how you know this? I know we're going back a long time back in time, but if you just could remember how it is that you know this, how you obtained this information.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had warned Murat Haxhocaj of the existence of that list. On operative of the State Security Service from Decani warned him that his name was on a list found during the search of the house of the Haradinaj family at Glodjane. He was told to be very careful where he went and that he had to inform us. When the murder happened, then we soon found out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson -- finish your answer before we give Mr. Emmerson ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the murder, members of his family informed us. I believe that it was actually his brother-in-law. And they reported him to be abducted and later killed, but it has been a long timing so -- and I think it was in October or November 1998. Anyway, towards the end of 1998 when he was killed, but I am speaking from memory now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be that given the number of caveats that this witness has placed around this portion of his evidence, and given the fact that it is unsourced, that it's not going to trouble Your Honours to any great extent in any event, but I have to make the point that this is information which is being elicited without any notice, without the Defence being given any advance indication, or having had any opportunity to prepare itself or investigate the allegation that's now being drawn through. And in those circumstances, it would be wrong, we submit, for the evidence to be included within any consideration of the testimony that's being given. It's simply being given off-the-cuff from memory without sources and, above all, without notice to the Defence, and that obviously would be fundamentally unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On the issue of notice, I was just following up on a question that one of the members of the Bench asked, and this is the answer I got from the witness and now which I'm simply seeking to clarify it. I wasn't intending to go into this issue, but it just came out in testimony and I am simply trying to clarify it. And it's also not new because the witness has in the past spoken about these lists, he did so in the previous testimony and it's also part of his statement. On the issue about the sources or the source of this information, the witness has explained to the best of his knowledge how he remembers this, and it's really just a matter for Your Honours at the end of the day to determine the weight to give to this specific evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As a general comment, may I simply say this, the ruling of the Trial Chamber in relation to this witness's evidence is that the testimony and exhibits that he gave at the original trial together with his Rule 65 ter statement are admitted into the record and that the Prosecution is entitled to lead additional evidence of which the Defence has been given notice in respect of the documents that it has now sought to tender through this witness. Obviously, there's no objection in relation to that. A slight danger for the way in which the evidence is being led is that counsel for the Prosecution are using -- is using documents as a spring-board to invite the witness to give broad-ranging testimony which is not based on the document or an explanation of the document of which the Defence has been given notice and which this Trial Chamber required the Defence to be given notice of, but merely to introduce a general topic and then to ask a series of wide-ranging questions about which no notice has been given which in one way or the other are said to flow from the document. But none of this testimony, none of this testimony, has any relationship to the document that's being exhibited or as to which notice has been given in accordance with the requirement that this Trial Chamber that notice should be given. And so we do respectfully ask Your Honours to keep this examination within the bounds of what is a proper explanation of documents that you have ordered can be admitted if proper notice is being given, rather than simply using these documents -- and it's a comment I haven't made before but it applies to much of the testimony that's been elicited, rather than simply using the document as a spring-board for generalised, wide-ranging testimony that is said in one way or another to derive from the document that, in fact, has no direct relationship to it, and this is a good example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Balaj, I join in those remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully, Mr. Emmerson's statement is not correct. We gave notice as to the areas we anticipated to cover in relation to each one of the documents that I have put to the witness during my examination, and this was done in the form of a supplemental information sheet which was disclosed to the Defence on Monday. So that is not correct. In relation to this specific topic of the lists that the witnesses has just spoken about, I was simply seeking a clarification on the basis of a question put by the Bench. It is not a new topic, so we -- we weren't anticipating going there, but it's not a new topic. It's an issue that was already addressed and on which the Defence have already asked questions in the last trial, it has already been dealt with before. So it's not a new topic for the Defence. But it's not correct to say that we did not give notice on the issues we expected to deal with. It's very clearly set out in the supplemental information -- clearly set out in the supplemental information sheet we disclosed to the Defence, and we're happy to provide a copy of that to Your Honours if there is an issue of dispute as to what we have given notice to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry. May I just take that one point out because we do have the information sheet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do say yesterday, Mr. Emmerson that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Anyway, you are objecting --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not objecting. I'm simply saying that my learned friend indicates that notice has been given of the topics that would be examined in relation to each document, that's true. But in relation to this document, for example, which is, after all, a document concerning the transfer of weapons, the witness -- the information sheet reads: "This witness indicates that the reference to Smajl in the document is a reference to Ramush Haradinaj. The witness doesn't know the author of the document but believes he was a person in charge of logistics based in northern Albania. The witness notes that the author of the document refers to the fact that persons were coming to him with Haradinaj's signature and requesting weapons and supplies. This information is consistent with information that the witness had at the time in relation to Haradinaj's role in the procurement of weapons." As one would expect, an indication of what it was sought to elicit in relation to that document. This testimony has nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may -- I don't think -- you are not asking for any ruling? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm simply asking that the -- that counsel do what you've already ordered that they should do, which is to confine the witness's testimony to an explanation of the documents that are being exhibited, none of which notice has been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one clarification, and this is a clarification to the statement. This is Exhibit P121, and if we could go to page 31 in both the English and the B/C/S and I'm looking for -- if we could zoom in the middle of the paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a reference here, and I direct your attention, sir, to Annex 71 --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry -- oh, I do apologise. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- which is one of the documents we tendered yesterday 65 ter 01003, and this is a document dated 6th August 1998, and it says in your statement that it's a DB report on the release of eight Serbs in July 1998 from Jablanica prison. I have a very simple question, sir. Yesterday, we were speaking about a surveillance operation your service conducted in the village of Jablanica in Djakovica municipality. Is the reference to Jablanica in your statement a reference to the same village, or is it a reference to a different village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the same village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That's all I had in relation to that paragraph. Thank you, Your Honours, that concludes my direct examination for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could we just revert to that passage from the witness's Rule 65 ter statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The passage which was just on the screen, Your Honour, that Ms. Kravetz was asking about, paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want, if I may, just to ask you some brief questions about the first part of paragraph 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, in doing this, I should make it clear to Your Honours that Annex 70 is not tendered by the Prosecution and is not exhibited in these proceedings and that the passage in this statement, though it remains in the statement, is therefore, for the purposes of these proceedings, unsourced nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, in that statement -- in that passage in paragraph 55, you refer as one of your sources to a statement made by a man called Naser Kalamashi to Djakovica SUP on the 5th of September, 1998, concerning the detention of between 17 and 20 people at Jablanica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you summarise parts of the statement, suggesting that the witness had said to officers of Djakovica SUP that Lahi Brahimaj had constructed a pool in a cellar filled with water and burnt motor oil in which detainees were forced to swim. Do you recall writing that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And then various other details said to come from that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I please call up document ID 06 -- sorry, 1D06-0037 ET. And if we can just enlarge it a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is an English translation, so I'm going to read to you the operative passages so that you can have them in translation, and I'll do so slowly. And perhaps I could ask you and Your Honours to bear in mind the date of the statement that you were referring to at paragraph 55, namely the 5th of September, 1998. This is a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor by Naser Kalamashi, dated the 26th of October, 2006. And if I can then, please, go over to the following page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this document was not notified to us at the beginning of the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Kravetz is correct that the document was only notified this morning because it was one that we turned up during the course of the witness's evidence, but it is a Prosecution witness statement of which they have been aware throughout both these proceedings and the previous trial. There's no prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Well, we should be made aware of documents according to the guide-lines Your Honours have issued, we should be made aware at the beginning of an examination of a witness of the documents the Defence intends to use. The Defence should not be allowed to simply pop up documents when they decide and when they're starting their cross-examination. We had no notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It's inevitable that during the course of a witness's testimony issues come up and come to be examined, and this is a document which, as I say, all parties have had and been aware. It's a Prosecution witness statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But at least if you didn't make the other party aware of it, then you make an application to add it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Oh, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- which you haven't done.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if I can add to this, this is also a document, given the fact that my learned colleagues were also present in the previous trial when this witness gave evidence, it's also a document they were aware of in the past, so they should have included it on their list. It's not a new document to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. But at least we can't comment on what happened in the previous case. We are concerned about this case. The guide-line does say at the beginning of -- at the taking of the solemn declaration the cross-examining party must give notice of the document. Of course if those documents are -- that notice is not given of a particular document, I think the prudent thing to do is to make an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for not having done so in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah, now the problem is what do we do about this. There's an objection against your use of this document because you didn't give notice of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can very easily read from it and without putting the document in I can put the question in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, reading from it is using it. You can put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I can put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to remove it from the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, i think it would be easier for Your Honours to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then you are using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so. I don't think -- I mean, if I can say so, the rule is obviously there for a reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is there for a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the reason is to prevent the Prosecution being taken by surprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This is not a document that the Prosecution is unaware of. It doesn't take them by surprise. It can be put in the form of a question where I simply read the operative passages from the witness statement and say -- and ask the question to the witness and then invite Your Honours at a later stage to admit it, or we can deal with it in a more convenient form which affords no prejudice to anybody. But I am in Your Honours' hands. I would invite you simply to allow me to continue with the cross-examination. It is very difficult to see what prejudice the Prosecution has suffered if it had been -- it's a purely technical objection. If it had been notified yesterday afternoon rather than this morning, Ms. Kravetz wouldn't have in any way altered the shape of her testimony -- of her evidence in chief and neither would she have had an opportunity to discuss it with the witness because the very purpose of the ruling is to ensure that that does not occur. So there's absolutely no prejudice. It is a purely technical objection. It is capable of being overcome by a rather cumbersome procedure of me simply reading it out. But I would respectfully suggest that the rule needs to be applied purposefully. The object is to prevent ambush so that the Prosecution has an opportunity to consider its position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. You use it, but make sure that next time you make an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour. Can we have it back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If we can pick it up at paragraph 9, first of all, Mr. Kalamashi tells the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'll read this slowly for you so that it can be interpreted: "I have never been a member of the KLA. I have no political affiliation. "Kodralija village never experienced the slightest KLA activities and I am hundred per cent sure that nobody in the village was KLA active or passive member. "On the 3rd of September, 1998," that, just to remind you, Mr. Stijovic, is just two days before the statement you were drawing your intelligence from. "On the 3rd of September, 1998, I was arrested and sentenced with one and a half years of imprisonment for illegal possession of weapons. Otherwise, I have no criminal background. "I would like to provide the ICTY representatives with more details regarding my arrest as mentioned above. "On 3rd of September, 1998, I remember the intensive offensive of Serbian forces took place in" our "area. The operation affected the villages of Bec, Kodrali, Rashkoc, Cermjan, and many others in our municipality. We were afraid to stay at home, since the house might be a target of shelling; therefore, our family was gathered in the field 300 metres far from my house. "We were siege by the Serbian army and police, and the males were ordered to take off the clothing and staying in underwears. In front of our family members, we were beaten with butts of Kalashnikovs, kicking by boots, and the Serbs were jumping on our backs, as we were ordered to lie down. Then we ... gathered on the road and this time we were beaten by paramilitary members. I believe that they were paramilitaries because they wore different camouflage uniforms than the police and army and wore red and black coloured bandannas over their heads. We were again beaten the same way as the army ..." Now, can I pause there. Can I take it, Mr. Stijovic, that you are familiar with the testimony that was given in the previous Haradinaj trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that question is a bit vague.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put the question more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which testimony are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put the question more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Have you studied, either during the course of the Haradinaj trial or since then, evidence given in that trial by anyone other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Have you read or followed the testimony of any witness who gave evidence in the previous trial?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And one would imagine, given your role as an intelligence officer, that you would follow that evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm retired now, but I'm interested in the situation and everything going on in Kosovo so I follow things.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you follow the testimony of Nebojsa Avramovic, the officer from Djakovica SUP who took these 11 men into custody?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- nor am I -- nor do I know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, as the Trial Chamber will, in due course, be aware, the SUP officer confirmed that 11 men were brought in on the 3rd of September wearing underclothes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mean to interrupt Mr. Emmerson. If we're going to be referring to previous testimony of a witness, we need references so we can all follow what Mr. Emmerson is reading. Also, I don't find it appropriate that he's putting testimony of a different person just like that to the witness without indicating exactly what he's meaning to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'll indicated what I'm meaning as the questions evolve, that's the purpose of cross-examination. But as to the objection that I shouldn't be putting other people's testimony to this witness, given that that's the sole purpose of this witness being called by the Prosecution, namely to put other person's often unsourced and secondary hearsay accounts through him, it's a rather strange objection to be putting. The relevance will become completely obvious. The transcript reference I'm dealing with is 6626, line 20; 6621, line 1; and 6622, line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that we're clear, the senior officer at Djakovica SUP who received these men gave evidence that they were brought in in their underwears, as Mr. Kalamashi's witness statement attests. Were you aware of that, that the man whose statement you referred to was brought in custody in his underwear?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware. I -- I had not heard of that type of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So that would be quite wrong, would it, if they had been beaten at the scene and taken in in their underwear before making the statement that you rely on, that would be quite wrong, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're adding -- you're adding the beating --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, the beating is in the passage in the statement I've just read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, I didn't hear that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The witness statement says he was beaten and with other men stripped naked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, in this -- in this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- yes, but not in the statement of Mr. -- what is his name, the other ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm coming to that, if I may. Because what Mr. Avramovic testified when asked whether they had been beaten is: Was it is possible that they had been?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you: Would it be completely wrong if those men were taken into custody in their underwear having been beaten?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, when you say "completely wrong," Mr. Emmerson, what do you mean, morally wrong or incorrect? Is it incorrect that that happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me put the question to the witness in an open form so he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate, in your view, for these men to have been taken into custody in their underwear? Stripped naked, in other words, by Serbian police and then taken into custody in their underwear. Would that be right or wrong in your view?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, if what you're saying is true, I think that it is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if what the senior SUP officer said in his evidence at the last trial was true, then what I've just put to you is true. So you can -- you can confirm to me that from the outset of the time in custody these men were being treated in a manner you regard as not right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness is in no position to confirm that. He's just been put the testimony of another witness and he's given the answer as -- he's explained as much as he knows, but he's in no position to be able to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I accept the complaint. I accept the challenge. Can I put another question in another way, a different question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was hypothetical, if what the [indiscernible] said --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, except that both parties to the incident say that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And perhaps the crucial question, Mr. Stijovic, is: You don't really know anything about the circumstances surrounding this, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just put to me as a question is something about which I have no knowledge. I don't know if it happened, but if it happened then it wasn't okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's very helpful. If it happened in the way described both by the police officer and the suspect, then obviously it wasn't okay. But do I understand the position to be: You don't really know anything about the circumstances of these men's detention; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, can I have it clearly on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Detention where?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Detention in SUP Djakovica during the period of time when the witness statement that the witness was summarising was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You don't know what was done to them, if anything, before that statement was taken, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I do know is that Naser Kalamashi's statement was taken in the Djakovica SUP, and I think I said that in my previous statement and I indicated which information had reached me from the Djakovica SUP. What was going on there, and if it's correct what that police inspector said, this senior officer, and what this statement and other statements say, well that's something that I really cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So you can't confirm one way or the other whether these men were tortured before they made their statements? You can't confirm that one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. First of all, the basis for -- there is no basis for this. My learned colleague has quoted only a portion of the statement of --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm coming on to the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- Mr. Avramovic in the previous case. He indicated that these persons were stripped-down to their underwear to be searched for weapons. Where this reference to torture comes from is not clear to me at the moment, and I don't -- I find it completely inappropriate that the witness was asked [Overlapping speakers] ... about it when he already stated that he knows nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me ask the questions in a different order, if my learned colleague is concerned about the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go back to the statement, please, and pick it up at paragraph 15 at the bottom of the stage after the men had been stripped naked and beaten:

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "We had to get on trucks and halfway to Gjakove the police came and we were ordered to get on police jeeps and taken to Djakovica SUP, then we were kept in the basement of the SUP premises for the following three days under constant beatings and torture. The police were coming to the basement and taking one by one for questioning. The interviews took place in the office on the 4th or 5th floor. I was arrested and kept there with other 11 co-villagers. "When I had been taken for interview in the office" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to read the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I am because it's obviously been translated for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "When I had been taken for interview in the office was sitting a man in civilian and asking questions in Serbian language. The only phrases he used in Albanian were as follows: 'Why are lying to us that you had not been KLA? Did you have an arm? Fuck your mother.' Then all questions were only in Serbian language which I did not understand. I had been interviewed for about ten of times but in different offices of Djakovica SUP HQ. But the interviewer was always the same and did not make any written notes. "During the interviews, apart from the interviewer, there were always present two other civilians who were beating me with baseball bats all over my body. On the 6th of September," that's the day after the statement you refer to, "I recall that a man, I do not remember whether in uniform or civilian clothing, came to the basement and ordered us to sign some document. We were asking if he has translator to read us what we are going to sign. The man replied: 'You will see translator.' Then we were beaten again and forced to sign document without knowing the content. "In October 2006, the ICTY ... read over to me a statement registered in the ICTY archives ... as I already said, it could be the same as I signed in the premises of SUP in Djakovica because I did never sign any other document. But I would like to raise my objections regarding the fact that I signed only one page. But the statement with the content I was acknowledged today is consisting of four pages. I would like to stress that there is no one word of true. I did not say anything what was mentioned in this statement as below ..." Now, if I've understood what you've told us already, correct me, Mr. Stijovic, you know nothing about the circumstances in which these men were detained; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know that they were detained. I don't have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, there's, as I said to you, testimony from the senior officer at SUP Djakovica that they were detained as well as the evidence in the statement you read. But the question I'm asking you is: If they were detained when the statement was taken that you relied upon, you don't know whether they were tortured or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but if you permit me, Your Honours, to say just a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, are they an answer to the question? I mean, I thought you'd answered the question. You don't know one way or the other; is that right? I mean, a minute ago you told us you didn't know anything about the detention, Mr. Stijovic. Did you or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a complex question. I cannot reply with a yes or a no to this question. If you permit me to say a couple of sentences, perhaps it will be clearer, with all due respect, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Before you do, Mr. Stijovic, before you add whatever it is you want to add, it is a very simple question and it is capable of an answer, yes or no. Do you know anything of the circumstances of the detention of these 11 men including Naser Kalamashi between the 3rd and the 6th of September, 1998? Do you know how they were treated during those three days, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you summarised the content of the statement and put forward its contents as reliable, you have no idea whether they're reliable or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess that's the end of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Let the record show that. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I remain in the same position that I was in prior to this gentleman taking the stand, and I reserve my right to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it he will be subject to re-call at some point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He will have to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some questions I can ask now, but I will also reserve my right to re-call this witness should additional information arise as a result of the inquiries that Mr. Guy-Smith has been making and which I have been supporting. May I -- could you give me just one moment to grab the -- I think there's a podium there that would be helpful to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stijovic. My name is Richard Harvey. I have the honour to represent Lahi Brahimaj. Let me just ask you, first of all, a little about the basis on which those working with you, under you, those who provided you with information, the basis on which that information was obtained. First of all, you used blackmail, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Please understand, Witness, when I say "you" in this context, I mean "you" collectively, the service for which you worked. You blackmailed witnesses into giving you information, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, in my previous testimony I talked about motives and how, in what way, the State Security Service got informants. You took a part of my explanation out of context and are insisting on that term, but my answer to that is no and I can explain the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I think your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: If we could have, please - yes, thank you - 04049, please, and if we could have page 18.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, the document is Exhibit P122.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Witness, if you could -- I could just read to you from the bottom of that page your answer at line 18: "A. We would create a compromising information -- or rather, compromising documents on the activity of a certain person. If it related to the co-operation with the KLA, then that was the information that we gained about these persons directly participating in KLA activities, in crimes, in criminal activities. And given the position that these people had within the KLA -- they were quite at a high level and were able to provide very important and relevant information to us. Then based on that, we would recruit them and introduce them to the Service." Over the page, please. "We would confront them with the information that we had about the incriminating activities that they were involved with, and then we asked them to do something for us in exchange for not being prosecuted, and they would do these things under the supervision and under the control of the State Security Service." Would you agree that that was blackmail?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the term "blackmail" is not quite appropriate in the sense of that meaning, but the answer does reflect one of the ways in which we recruited informants from the KLA to work for our interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Let's go back to page 17, please. Thank you. Again your answer at the bottom of that page: "The motivation of these people in their work for the State Security Service was diverse, just like anywhere else. The basic element was money. The second possible motive was of a political nature, where they did not agree or they disapproved of various activities. And the third motive was to compromise somebody. If somebody -- if we had information about somebody that was of a compromising nature, then we would" over the page, please, "resort to blackmailing. I'm using that term because this is what it amounts to everywhere else in the world." Now, Witness, do you wish to change the answer you gave this Court a short while ago?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps clarify it. Yesterday, in answer to the question, Did I listen to the transcript, I did. I listened to 20 hours of audio, and I said yesterday perhaps that I would change the wording of some things, and you can check that. I said that in the transcript. I can clarify this particular matter if it's imprecise, if you insist on that particular detail with an illustration of a classic example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not asking you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, I realise you are probably going to be some time with this witness on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I know this may be an inopportune moment, but it's the time. Would you like to continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. But before we take the break, may the witness please be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I will do as soon as there's someone to proceed with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Harvey. May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I might get further this way, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. It's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, one of the means of information-gathering that you used was electronic surveillance and listening to telephones; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Specifically you said that you monitored telephone conversations of Lahi Brahimaj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. We specifically listened in on the telephone used by his mother in his family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And did that continue throughout until the month of August 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When did it stop?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In April or May, the reports became less frequent and then there was this police and army operation to break-up the strongholds of the KLA. So then there was no more need to monitor the phones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, the operation to break-up the stronghold in Jabllanice took place at the beginning of August of 1998; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in order to be precise, sir, this was an operation carried out by the police and the army which began in June 1998, and it finished in late August/early September in that border area towards Jablanica, towards Albania, Jablanica, Junik, and so on. So the operation finished in late August and early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would you agree that the forces that you have just mentioned, the forces of the police and the army, did not enter Jabllanice before August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And so, would you accept, therefore, that you would have continued to listen to and monitor the telephone usage of the Brahimaj family until that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Your Honours, I said that until April/May we had certain information which were of interest and useful to us. After that, these reports became less frequent, and it was obvious that the other side assumed or knew that their phone conversations were being monitored. So the things that we were getting were of less importance to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not the answer to the question, Mr. Stijovic. The question was: Would you accept that you would have continued to listen to and monitor the telephone usage of the Brahimaj family until that time, that time being August 1998. You should either be saying: Yes, we did; or no, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you've also told us, I believe, that if not on this occasion but on the last occasion when you testified, you said that Lahi Brahimaj could not move by day because of your surveillance techniques; he had to confine his movements to moving by night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we just have a reference to the passage my learned colleague is citing to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just give me one moment. It would be at page 9244 of the transcript which is at page 358 of Exhibit 04049. "He was not allowed to leave Jablanica, but rather -- "He was not allowed to leave Jablanica, but rather only moved overnight in the surrounding villages."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is that the position, that he was only able to move at night-time, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm saying what you read about what I said in my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your answer. Is your previous testimony on this point correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you also monitoring radio telephones used by Mr. Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We monitored the telephones and the radio traffic used -- that was used. I don't know whether that was his personal phone or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you were asked on the last occasion - I'm looking at page 8915 of the transcript, which is at page 48 of Exhibit 04049 - you were asked last time: "What happened to the transcripts or the tapes of the conversations, telephone conversations and electronic surveillance, that you listened to?" And you gave this answer: "I can't give you an answer to that question. I know that these documents and transcripts were made, that there are recordings of these conversations, and as to where they are located, I wouldn't be able to say. I think you need to direct that question to the authorities in Belgrade and ask them where this documentation is located." You were further asked: "Do you believe them still to exist?" And you responded: "I am convinced that a large portion of these documents exists. I know that in the eve of the bombing, we pulled out quite a lot of documents from Kosovo and Metohija and we moved them to safe areas in" -- I'm sorry, I don't have the next page, I think it's Belgrade. Anyway, do you recall being asked those questions and giving those answers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And have you made any attempt to check on whether those transcripts or tape-recordings do still exist, since you testified last time in preparation for your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You would have known as a result of listening to telephone communications when Mr. Brahimaj was in Jabllanice and when he wasn't in Jabllanice to a reasonable extent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you would also have known -- well, let me ask it this way: Did you monitor the communications from the General Staff of the KLA in the Berisha mountains area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main KLA staff was at Mount Berisa at one point, but it was very mobile. It moved around in the Drenica area. So the direct answer to this question would be: Yes, we did monitor them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you were aware that Lahi Brahimaj was a member of that General Staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't in the KLA Main Staff. He was an officer, so-called liaison officer, between the Dukadjin Operative Zone and the KLA Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Are you not aware that he was a member of the General Staff in charge of logistics and finances?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not in the KLA Main Staff. That I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you follow the evidence given by Mr. Zyrapi in the last trial?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll stay on and listen to his evidence today then. Thank you. May I ask you this: As you were listening to the telephone of Lahi Brahimaj's mother, you - and I mean collectively you in the RDB and the other forces of the Serb Republic - you must have been aware that she and her 105-year-old mother were alone in the house when Serb forces attacked at the beginning of August; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. It is not correct that we wire-tapped Lahi Brahimaj's mother's telephone. We wire-tapped the family telephone because of Lahi Brahimaj, because of him, not because of his mother or because of this elderly lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question: By tapping that phone, you must have been aware that Mr. Brahimaj's elderly mother and extremely elderly grandmother were alone in that house at the time that Serb forces attacked Jabllanice at the beginning of August 1998; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. Based on tapping a phone, you cannot know who else is in the house unless the person speaking on the phone says so. The only thing that you can hear is what that person says and the person at the other end and what -- the things they say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And based on not only the telephone tapping, but the other surveillance methods that you employed, you must have been aware that the KLA had effectively left Jabllanice at the time of the attack in August of 1998, mustn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA withdrew from Jablanica. They had withdrawn. But they were present in the neighbouring villages. They moved in reaction to the movements of the forces of the police in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And who was in charge of the operation to attack Jabllanice?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know who was in charge --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Were you involved in the planning of that operation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not only the Jablanica operation. There was a joint staff made up of members of the MUP and the army at Kosovo level, and they co-ordinated the actions. The individual actions in the field were in charge of operative commanders. I don't know who the commander of the unit was that was active in any particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would it be accurate to say that Lahi Brahimaj and his family were a specific target of that operation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One couldn't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: One specific target, not the specific target, of attacking Jabllanice was to take out the Brahimaj family, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You used the term "liquidate" this morning at page 4 of your testimony in relation to people bringing arms into the country. This was an operation to liquidate the KLA in Jabllanice, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is more precise. It was indeed an operation, the purpose of which was to destroy, or liquidate - or whichever term you prefer to use - for the destruction of the KLA forces that were active in that area, to rout them and destroy them. And you can choose whichever term you prefer to describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And was it part of the plan that if you couldn't liquidate the KLA, you would ensure that anybody in Lahi Brahimaj's family, including his mother and his grandmother, would be murdered in cold blood?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is an ugly insinuation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: The ugly thing is that they were cut to pieces and murdered in the most horrific fashion, and you know that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, sir, but I heard it from you or one of your colleagues from the Defence. I was unaware of that and I am indeed sorry if such a thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No investigation took place under your direction into any - and I'll use a nice word - misconduct by the troops who invaded Jabllanice, did it? No investigation took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I find it rather confusing especially at this moment in your cross-examination, the way you use the word "you." Sometimes it's the service and sometimes it's this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: It's a fault of the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would you please make the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: If we were speaking French, it would be much easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You -- when I use "you," of course I know that you personally as an individual did not enter Jabllanice; I am correct in that, aren't I?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You understood that when I was saying "you" in this context, I was referring to "you" collectively as the group responsible for that attack in which you individually played a role in the planning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not how I understood you. I understood what you said as something very bad, indeed. And in my previous testimony, I said what I knew about this event. Only in 2007, before Judges of this Tribunal, I said that I only then heard of the event, if it indeed ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just briefly in relation to the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Serbia. That gave you and those who worked with you the power to hold people for 72 hours, and, in fact, that could be extended to a total of 96 hours for interrogation. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That law was in force at the time, I mean the Law on Criminal Procedure, and, yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And people were interrogated for periods of four days, 96 hours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know well that it is very difficult to interrogate somebody for 96 hours. That's the total period of time that person spent on the premises of the police. The interrogation itself was much shorter. It depended on the mental and physical abilities of the person in question. You would have to be Superman to interrogate somebody for 96 hours or to answer -- to be interrogated for that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, you would interrogate them certainly from 8.00 in the morning until 10.00 at night; that happened, didn't it, for four consecutive days?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such situations. In a situation like that, we were mindful of the physical and mental condition of the person in question, and depending on that the -- our staff who conducted the interrogation would adapt the process. But yes, there were situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you're well aware that many complaints were made of people being tortured physically, brutally beaten in the course of such very intensive interrogations. You're well aware of those complaints, aren't you? Whether you believe them or not, you're aware that complaints were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, is this you personally or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: This is you personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could I suggest to avoid this kind of confusion that you use "your services" when you don't mean you personally, for instance, or something like that. Because it's really confusing, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'll try, and I apologise for any confusion I may have caused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You personally were aware of complaints of torture, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
