utterances.text: Yes, there were such complaints, but, for example, Naser Kalamashi never complained in 2000 or 2001 or 2002, 2003, or 2004. Only in 2006 did he deny what he had said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He didn't complain to his torturers, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Harvey. Madam Kravetz, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I do have some questions, Your Honour. I do want to point out that since my learned colleagues have reserved the right for further cross-examination, I'll just be cross-examining on the questions put to the witness today, but there may be need for further re-examination at a later stage if the witness is re-called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, today, my colleague, Mr. Harvey, put a series of questions to you - and it starts at page 35 of the transcript and goes on to page 36 - in relation to a statement you made in your previous testimony in the Haradinaj trial to the use of -- or resort to blackmailing. And I'm reading from page 36 of the transcript, lines 11 and 12, you said: "I can clarify this particular matter, if it's imprecise, if you insist on that particular detail with an illustration of a classical example." I wanted to ask you, sir, if you could clarify and indicate what you meant, actually, by the use of this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instead of the word "blackmail," you could use the word "choice." If we suppose a hypothetical situation in which there are persons A and B who are members of the KLA and they are friends --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. The witness is now starting to talk in terms of "if you suppose." We don't -- we're not here for fairytales, we're here for evidence, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking -- you indicated that you wanted the opportunity to clarify this reference you had made earlier with an illustration of a classic example, and I just wanted you to clarify that, as you had indicated in response to questions of my colleague, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to do that, so if you allow me to finish. Persons A and B are KLA members. B is married and in prison due to his activities. The State Security Service gets information and has documentary proof of a close relationship between persons A and B. We draft documents about that and face person A with the information we have and tell that person that we will inform the spouse of person B. And that is how we got information. So we gave a person a choice whether they would opt for a conflict with the family or the alternative, but there were also other situations in which a person commits a misdemeanour against law and order and that person works abroad. For that reason, a -- the -- their passport is taken away from them and that is why the person cannot return in time to his or her work-place in western Europe. We, as the State Security Service, were able to be lenient and return the passport to that person in time for them to return to their work-place. If that is blackmail, all right. This is one of the methods we applied. Is that blackmail or facing -- or offering a choice to a person is something that's open to interpretation. I don't know if I was clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Ms. Kravetz continues and it may have been entirely obvious to Your Honours what it was the witness was trying to say between lines 5 and line 15, but I think he may have got his As and Bs mixed up. Because if one reads the transcript, he talks about the State Security Services knowing about a relationship, a close relationship between A and B, and it is hypothetical A and B were the two KLA members, rather than the spouse and the other one. I think it may be obvious what he meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I think we heard what he said. All I just wanted to ask you, Mr. Stijovic, is: In that example of A and B, that whole exercise -- that whole explanation, that whole situation that you explained to us, what do you call that in one word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I call it choice. Either you'll work for us or we will disclose all this -- all these immoral things to your friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was in one word. You said "choice." Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The relationship was between the wife of A and B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can call it blackmail. It only occurred to me now. I'm trying to find another appropriate term in Serbian but I'm unable to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what I could call it. I'm asking you what you call it in one word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blackmail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a series of questions about the witness statement of Naser Kalamashi, which is referred to in your -- your own witness statement. When your service obtained information through witness statements, was there a process through which your service verified or cross-checked the information contained in those statements; and if yes, could you explain what that process was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a procedure and talking about the statement of Mr. Kalamashi that we got through the SUP of Djakovica, it was important for us to learn that there was a prison at Jablanica. Through other activities, that is, interviews with other sources and other information, we verified the truthfulness of the information about there being a prison at Jablanica. Some Serbs, Montenegrins, Roma, and Albanians had been kidnapped and abducted. To me as an analysis, that information was extremely important, the existence of a prison where there were kidnapped persons and that prison being in the village of Jablanica. That information was additionally checked through live sources, through technical means, and everything that the State Security Service could resort to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Your Honour. Just for purposes of clarity of the record, there's an acronym which is going to be used here which is SUP. I'm wondering if we could get some just clarification of what that means specifically. I believe there are a number of acronyms that have been used by this gentleman with regard to his testimony, SUP, MUP, and some others things, which people may internally have knowledge of, but they may not necessarily be reflected in the record so that the Chamber is aware specifically of what these entities mean. The reason I think that could be of some importance goes directly to some of the questions Judge Delvoie was asking with regard to the issue of "you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, we will do that. Mr. Stijovic, what does the acronym SUP stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SUP stands for secretariat of the interior in Djakovica. There was a Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia which had two departments: One was public security, and the lower organisational units of which were the SUPs; and there was the department of state security, which had as lower-ranking units centres of state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what were they called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the state security centres?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The lower-ranking units centres of the state security, what were they called? You told us the other were called SUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Centres. Centres of the state security department. For -- to clarify for the gentleman, the MUP of the Republic of Serbia had SUPs, that is, secretariats of the interior; below which there are OUPs, organs of the interior; and below that, there are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter says: Could you please slow down. He's struggling to keep pace with you. Then you have introduced a couple of other acronyms now and I would like to hand you back to Madam Kravetz. You were stopped where you were saying "below which there are OUPs, organs of the interior; and below that, there are ..." Can you continue from there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You can continue, sir. You were talking about OUPs, and "below that, there are ...," and just complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police departments. Below the OUPs, there were police departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, that clarifies that. I want to go back to the answer you gave when I asked you whether the information was verified or cross-checked. You said at lines 7 and 8 of page 50, you said: "Through other activities, that is, interviews of other sources and other information, we verified the truthfulness of their information about there being a prison at Jablanica." Could you just clarify for the Court what you meant when you said "and other information." Which other information were you speaking about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June, in the area of Dubovik, we arrested a number of persons, and after interviewing them, we got information that the KLA group that was active in Dubovik, which is in the Pec municipality, in mid-June 1998, three persons were kidnapped, two Serbs and Montenegrins, Novica Vujisic and Vucic Vuckovic, who are related, and a Muslim, Izet Gutic. These persons had been kidnapped by members of the Shalja family who ran the KLA organisation at Dubovik. Their property was destroyed, their vehicle was taken by a KLA member from Dubocak, which is a hamlet of Dubovik. And those persons were taken to the Jablanica prison by a KLA member whose nickname was Sadam [phoen]. According to our information, it also happened in July to Milos Rajkovic, a man who at the time was about 50 years old. He was also taken to the Jablanica prison. And we know nothing about their fate to this date, if I'm not mistaken. There was more such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I will -- it may be that the witness is finished, but I've been listening to it, I'm in Your Honours' hands. But it's entirely open to the Chamber to bring a stop to this because this evidence is plainly outside anything which has been notified. It's unsourced, and it's vulnerable to all the same objections as to reliability and cross-reliability, as all of the other issues that have been brought up. I mean, this is really barrel-scraping stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join in that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I most certainly join in that objection. Apart from anything else, the witness has been asked about other information. He says discusses with other sources at page 50, line 8, he was -- had been asked by Ms. Kravetz and she correctly came back and tried to get him to explain again what he meant about sources other than from interviews. And what he, I suggest, euphemistically refers to as interviews, sessions in which people are interrogated at great length --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes, I will stop doing that. But I think the witness's attention should also be drawn to the fact that every time one of those interviews occurred, there appears in the statement that accompanies it or the official note of the interview the expression "source unreliable, information partially verified." And all of these in my submission, all of those so-called interviews, yield nothing except what the interviewer wants out of it and have to be regarded as completely unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are really submissions to be made at a later stage when the time comes for Your Honours to assess the weight of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or they could be tendered into evidence through the witnesses. Madam Kravetz was asking a question -- a follow-up question on which arose in cross-examination and which elicited an answer which the witness -- in which the witness said -- I'm looking for those interviews and information, if somebody can tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Page 50, line 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Right -- said -- that is the question at page 49, line 24: "Sir, you were asked a series of questions about the witness statement of Naser Kalamashi which is referred to in your own witness statement. When your service obtained information through witness statements, was there a process through which your service verified or cross-checked the information contained in those statements; and if yes, could you explain what that process was?" Now, since I came to this Tribunal, when questions are asked I have found that, first of all, questions are asked in the page form, answers are given in ten-page form. Now, that's why I have been insisting, for instance, when I'm asking a question, I say: You can either say yes or no, because I don't want a further explanation. Now, I think if there was any objection to be raised, it must be raised against the form of the question. Unfortunately, when the witness now, in answer to that question, goes for 1, 2, 3, 4 -- 10 lines and comes up with evidence that you hadn't had notice about, whose fault is that? I -- okay. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if we were engaged in a proper form of question and answer, then the fault would lie at the feet of the questioner. If the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the objection must be made at the time when the question is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But we have been -- and I'm assuming, and perhaps I'm making a mistake with regard to experience in many -- in many courtrooms, but in my experience has been a -- both affirmative and negative with regard to the Tribunal. We're not allowed to object to an answer. If an answer is non-responsive to a question, then, in fact, that answer should not be continued nor should it be made part of the record. But I have been in situations previously -- and I was, as a matter of fact -- I've had an argument specifically with one of the members of this Chamber with regard to that particular issue. So if -- so if the question that is posed is either posed sloppily or artfully - and it can be one or the other - and it elicits the kind of rambling responses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It could also just be a plain question: What's your name, and then you get -- given [Overlapping speakers] ... page answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If the question is: What is your name? And I answer that question by saying: Well, when there was a disenfranchisement of the Kosovar Albanian people in 1990 as a result of legislation that came through, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, then as a questioner, if Mr. Mair, for example, was asking me that question, it would be Mr. Mair's responsibility at that point in time to say: Excuse me, Mr. Guy-Smith, but you're not responding to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: If we were -- and I've spent many years practicing in the United States - the appropriate move there would -- a motion to strike --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Would be a motion to strike as non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, it's not a bad jurisdiction to operate in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But the point I'm making is that essentially Your Honours are -- should be invited to completely ignore an answer that is non-responsive and that's what I would invite you to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is what we do do when we look at the judgement -- when we write the judgement. But, you know, we can't get the witness -- what I usually do say is I say to counsel: Counsel, control your witness. And I've said it already in this trial, and I've said it already to this counsel before. But, you know, I can only say it so many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we were being thin-skinned. We thought that you were telling us that we should have objected to her question before hearing the answer was non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whatever it is. Well, anyway, you may proceed, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, just going back to my question, and I would like you to focus on the question I'm asking. You have already told us that interviews were one of the sources that you used in your work and you have referred to other information. And what I'm trying to clarify is what you meant when you referred to "other information."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Kravetz, do you ask this in a general way or with respect to something very specific?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I didn't want to restate the whole question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think after all this, the witness knows that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So, sir, we were talking about how your service cross-checked or verified information that was contained in witness statements that you received. And you said that you did this through interviews with other sources and "other information." What I'm seeking to clarify and get an answer from you is: Which other information did you use to verify or cross-check what was contained in the witness statements that your service received?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SUP reports that we received, information we received through the public media in Albanian, information we received that originated from the army intelligence service, foreign journalists who were in that area, we used all available sources which could point out to us something happening or some information that was unclear to us or in order to deepen our knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that clarifies that. And just going back to your answer on page 50, line 10, you referred to "some Serbs, Montenegrins, Roma, and Albanians had been kidnapped and abducted." Can you explain where these persons were kidnapped and abducted in a very concise way, if you can?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STIJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The abductions occurred in the triangle in the operative zone of Dukadjin, the municipalities of Pec, Decani, Djakovica, Klina, the area of these four municipalities. I mentioned abductions in the villages of Dubovik and Raosic [phoen]. There was an abduction of a financial expert near the village of Dujak in the municipality of Djakovica. Radunovic from Pec, he was an economist. We had an abduction of Stosic --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Objection on precisely the same terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just simply seeking to clarify the answer because in the way it currently stands on the transcript it's not completely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The point is -- the point being made, Madam Kravetz, is once you have got your answer, stop your witness. The answer I think ended at: "The abductions occurred in the triangle of the operative zone of Dukadjin, the municipalities of Pec, Decani, Djakovica, Klina, the area of these four municipalities." Full stop. There you must cut him.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I, in fact, would go further to the root of the problem. The root of the problem is that the permissible cross-examination question and answer is what methodology in general did you use to cross-verify? The witness answered that question by referring to a list of sources, including foreign journalists. That's the answer to the question. What Ms. Kravetz is really trying to do is to elicit specific examples. And the clarification, as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Emmerson. She had moved beyond that. She just wanted to know -- the next question was: Where were these people kidnapped --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: She had dealt with the methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm objecting to that question. I'm objecting to her introducing specific examples --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you should have objected as the question was being asked at that stage. That's what I'm just saying. That's the question you are objecting to. The question was -- sorry: "Can you explain where these persons were kidnapped and abducted in a very concise way, if you can?" Page 58, lines 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. The reality is that all of this testimony which is designed to be elicited to give specific examples, all of it unsourced and unnotified, is beyond the scope of proper re-examination. The only legitimate cross-examination question that triggers this line of re-examination - re-examination must be directed to questions asked in cross-examination - concerns Ms. Kravetz's attempt to repair the damage caused by this witness's acknowledgement that when advancing as reliable a statement of Bekim -- Naser Kalamashi in his witness statement, he had no idea, as he acknowledged, whether it was reliable or not. That was the question in cross and the answer. And any re-examination must be properly directed to that. Now obviously she can't ask him anything about that particular statement because that would impeach his original answer. So what she's entitled to do is ask what the methodology in general was. She's asked that. It's been answered. And all of this specific material trawled from a witness who has no sources available to him or to us or to Your Honours is way beyond legitimate re-examination and should be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully, my question falls squarely within the scope of re-examination. I had picked up from a question that was put by Mr. Emmerson to the witness in relation to a statement, and at this point I am simply seeking to clarify the answer he gave and I'm entitled to do that, to clarify the answer, just so it's understandable when Your Honours go back and read the transcript of this witness and his response to my question. It was a simple clarificatory question that I put to the witness, and I'm entitled to do that. I wasn't seeking to elicit specific examples. I was only asking for where these persons were abducted and the witness has answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, objection upheld.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, at this stage I have no further questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stijovic, thank you so much for coming to testify at the Tribunal. You have now come to the end of your testimony. You are excused. You may stand down, but before you stand down I just want to mention this, that certain arrangements are still pending. So realise that Mr. Guy-Smith has not cross-examined you. You may very well be re-called to come back for cross-examination by Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Harvey. Just to let you know so you are not surprised when you are called again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that regard, could the Chamber kindly admonish him with regard to who he can have contact with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because of that, you've got to remember that even though you're now being excused, you are still under -- bound by the declaration you made to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. But more importantly, because you are still on the witness-stand, you may not discuss this case with anybody, in particular with none of the people in the Prosecution side, but nobody until you are finally excused. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So until you are excused, you may not discuss the case with anybody. Okay. Until you are finally excused from further testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Your Honour, could you please explain to me this: Am I going home now or am I staying here? I mean, it can take a year for me not to be able to speak about my testimony with anybody. I mean, after all, this is a public testimony. I testified publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are going home now, but it will not take a year, it will not take six months, it will not take a month, it will not take two weeks. Okay. Thank you so much. You are now excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we move to the next witness, my colleague, Ms. Goy, would like to make an oral application which concerns an upcoming witness this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but as a matter of logic, before we move on to Ms. Goy's application or notification, can I just make absolutely certain that Your Honours have understood in relation to the witness statement, the 65 ter witness statement, of the last witness -- and it may be absolutely clear but it wasn't necessarily as clear on the transcript when Mr. Dixon explained it as I'd like it to be for Your Honours. The 65 ter statement purports to exhibit a large number of documents and to comment on them. Now, because of decisions taken by the Prosecution in this trial based, in large part, on rulings of admissibility by the previous Trial Chamber, a large number of those documents that the witness purports to exhibit and describe are not, in fact, being tendered in these proceedings. So if I can just give Your Honours an example. If we could -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just be -- you are aware that at the beginning of the testimony of this witness -- and Madam Kravetz did ask to tender into evidence the documents that the parties don't object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then she proceeded to tender the documents that have not been tendered in the previous case.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the previous trial, which is what she did. So I'm not sure when you say "a large number of documents have not been tendered," I'm not quite sure what --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me explain because I think it is perhaps confusing. There are three categories of exhibited documents. There are those that were tendered in the previous trial but ruled inadmissible, with one exception, the Prosecution has not sought the re-introduction of those documents in this trial. That one exception has been re-introduced by agreement. Then there are new documents that were never tendered in the previous trial, and those are the ones that have been tendered in oral testimony. So essentially, what has been -- what -- the documents that have been put before Your Honours mirror identically the documents that were ruled admissible by the previous Trial Chamber with the exception of one document which is now admitted by agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the ones that were not admitted at all in the previous trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They are -- no, the ones that were not -- oh, yes, I'm sorry, the completely new documents, those that weren't tendered in the previous trial. Your Honour is quite right. If I can just give Your Honours an illustration because it is quite important to get this right. I don't know whether you have a hard copy of the witness's 92 ter statement at hand, but, if not, somebody will give me the correct reference for calling it up. Here it is. It's P121.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So if we call up P121. It is rather important as Your Honours read through the statement. You'll see why in just a moment. I'm sorry, it's not appearing on my screen. Very well. Can I ask, please, that we turn to -- at the bottom of the page is numbered 1 of 36. Can we move to page 25 of 36, just as an illustration for Your Honours. Now, towards the bottom of that page, I don't know whether Your Honours can see -- ah, yes, just halfway down that paragraph. Annex 45 -- towards the bottom end. Annex 45, if you highlight that until the end. Annex 45 is a -- I'm sorry, we've lost it: "Annex 45 is a Pec DB report dated 1st of April, describing what was found in the Haradinaj family compound when it was searched by MUP forces, including lists of individuals to be 'liquidated because they were supposedly Serbian spies.'" Now, that document is not in evidence. It was ruled inadmissible, and it's not tendered by the Prosecution in these proceedings. So, for example, on the question of lists, the evidence is the evidence of the witness, that there was a list, it had names on, the names on cross-checking with Serbian RDB files were names of individuals who were, in fact, whether through blackmail or bribery, collaborators. Now, if one looks at this passage, it -- the report then summarises what else is in the document, and similarly, one goes on with Annex 46 is a DB Pec official note dated -- of an interview of Rasim Sulejmani, and it goes on the following page and describes it. Now, there are numerous passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They're not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, they're not tendered, but I wouldn't want Your Honours when reading the statement to be under the illusion that there is any evidence from the witness at all -- you see, simply from reading the statement one does not get a distinction between what is and is not tendered. So the approach which we would invite Your Honours to take is that insofar as the documents that are in -- referred to and described in the witness statement are not tendered by the Prosecution, Your Honours can effectively strike through the operative paragraphs in the 92 ter because they're entirely unsourced. That's essentially the position. I just wanted to make sure that was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Madam Kravetz, you were saying something?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're not seeking to rely on the exhibits that were not tendered, and I think Your Honours when reading through this evidence will be able to assess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much for that. I thought you were telling us something before Mr. Emmerson rose.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I was, Your Honours. I was just saying that before we move on to the next witness, my colleague, Ms. Goy, would like to make an oral application, and it concerns a protected witness who is scheduled for later on in the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Goy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Should we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I would like to make an application in relation to the protective measures of Witness 78, and we had to notify the Defence yesterday evening about that, and I would like to do that in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Goy. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution calls Bislim Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to come in, we've been given -- I hear you calling ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you're referring to the bundle, I can clarify that. There's certain documents which we considered would be more efficiently shown to the witness in hard copy, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. No, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Zyrapi. You may now be seated. Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: My name is Bislim Zyrapi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Would you please state your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: 9th of July, 1962 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I was born in Studenqan village, the Suhareke community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you provide the Office of the Prosecutor at this Tribunal with a statement in November 2005 and another statement in April 2007?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, did you testify in the initial Haradinaj trial in April 2007?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if we could call up, Your Honours, 65 ter Exhibit 00117 on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the information in this document is correct as of today's date?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me direct you to your current occupation. Is that your current occupation as referred in the document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At the time, I was a director of the department. I no longer exercise this function. As to the rest of it, the rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this document. It was -- it's one of the associated documents, but there was just the correction that needed to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P158.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, sir, after arriving in The Hague, have you had a chance to review your prior testimony from the Haradinaj trial?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And having reviewed that testimony, are you satisfied that it accurately reflects what you said at the time when you provided the testimony?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, if you were asked the same questions today as you were when you testified, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would move to admit 65 ter 04004, which is this witness's testimony from the initial Haradinaj trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 04004 will be Exhibit P159.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, after arriving in The Hague, have you had a chance to review the statements which you gave the Office of the Prosecutor in November 2005 and April 2007?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And having reviewed those statements, do they accurately reflect what you said at the time when you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And if questions were put to you about the subject matter in those statements, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with that, I would move to admit 65 ter Exhibit 118 and 121, which are the statements referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Statements 118 and 121 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given each an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 00118 will be Exhibit P160, and 65 ter 00121 will be Exhibit P161.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would also move for the admission of the associated exhibits that accompany the statements and transcript. We've notified that to the Registry on the 23rd and the Defence on the 22nd of August, so all of those exhibits with the exception of 65 ter 00117, which is previously admitted obviously at the start of the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was the response of the Defence on those exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, I've only heard from the Haradinaj Defence team, and they've indicated that they don't object. I haven't heard from the other two Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Guy-Smith is on his feet. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the associated exhibits that are on the original -- that are written exhibits that are in the original language, Albanian and/or Serbian, we have no objection. With regard to the translations that will be made available to the Court, to the extent they have not been changed or modified from those translations that were previously a part of the record in a similar situation that we were yesterday, once again we have no objection. With regard to those modified or new translations that have been made by the Prosecution, we do have an objection and we believe there are somewhere in the neighbourhood of about ten of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response, Mr. Menon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, to the extent that translations have been revised, it's -- it would have been because -- and I'm not able to specifically refer to anything because Mr. Guy-Smith hasn't specifically referred to any exhibits that he -- that troubled him. But to the extent that there have been revisions, it's because there were either errors or the translation was not as precise as it needed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Menon, would be: Who did the revision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that would depend on the specific document. I'm not in a position actually to address that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I mean is -- I'm not asking for the person, but which section of the Tribunal did the revision?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can I just have a moment to consult with my colleague, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is that for those exhibits that had translations that were done internally within the Office of the Prosecutor, then the revision process stayed within the Office of the Prosecutor. For those translations that were originally done by CLSS, then any revisions would have been done by CLSS. We're obviously in Your Honour's hands. If Your Honours would prefer that all revisions be done through CLSS, then we can make that arrangement. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be the preference of the Chamber, I would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there is another problem with regard to the manner in which my opponent is suggesting we proceed, which is there is an exhibit which is part of the record, and to change that translation at this time is inappropriate. That was why I rose yesterday, for the exact same reason with regard to Ms. Kravetz's attempt to engage in the exact same behaviour. And as a matter of fact, with regard to the revised -- at least the internal revised translation of one document, that's 65 ter 00140, it is -- there are substantial changes with regard to the meaning. So I think that we're in a very simple situation. They had an exhibit, they're relying on the exhibit, the exhibit should go in as it went in before, and to deviate from that position at this point in time is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, please assist me. I understand perfectly the logic of your position, that if the Prosecution is relying on an item that was previously tendered and it has been changed by translation, we're dealing with something else and technically they can't do that because it's something different. But in purely practical terms, if the revised translation for the reasons Mr. Menon has mentioned has been done by CLSS, not the OTP or anybody else, mustn't the presumption of the correctness and probity and everything of CLSS override the logic of your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The answer to that question is no, which I wouldn't have expected it to be except having dealt in my previous case with a native-born attorney. The number of times that we had serious and substantial arguments or disagreements about the meaning of a word or a phrase with CLSS were legion and we were constantly in the process of trying to iron this out, and I was surprised at the number of times that, quite frankly, I would say that our view - because theoretically I'm advocating - but our view won the day because it, in fact, was an appropriate translation of either the word or the concept. It's unfortunate, but as we all know there is an old statement which is -- and I'm going to paraphrase it at this point, which is that the translation is treason. And by that, there are often difficulties that one has between the original language and it being translated into another language. We've actually, as a matter of fact, seen that earlier today with the use of the word "you." I mean, I wish I -- what I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I follow you. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just correct the record. For the record, Mr. Guy-Smith referred to 65 ter 00140. My understanding is that the translation that was relied upon in the initial trial is still the translation that is in e-court and it remains a draft translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It looks like --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It seems to me, if I might, Your Honour, because it's not all of the documents. There are a discrete number of documents. Perhaps I can get together with my opponent at some point during some break and we can iron out these specific issues, if it comes to that, or we can iron out the issues and see where it goes from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying. In my view, there are two separate issues here. There is the point you make, Mr. Guy-Smith, about what - for lack of a better word - I'll call incorrectly translated translation that has gone into evidence in a previous hearing, and that's a separate issue from either corrections being made by CLSS or internally within the OTP. I would imagine that assuming there was no prior trial, what went -- whatever is being translated should be translated by CLSS. If there is a dispute between the parties about -- or between the parties and CLSS about the meaning of a particular word or phrase, they can take it up with CLSS and CLSS can confirm that the party is correct and therefore CLSS acquires in that correction by the party. However, if an incorrectly translated document went into evidence in the prior trial, it seems inappropriate to correct it, unless the parties agree. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I agree with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope I can represent the entire Bench correctly here. What Judge Delvoie is putting across is that it would be preferable if, even if a document has gone in incorrectly in the prior testimony, it would be preferable if a mistake is discovered to know what the correct mistake is. However, there would be a caveat to say we separate that from what is the evidence that was tendered in the previous case so that we understand what was put before the Court in the previous case but we also have an understanding of the correct interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have no difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I have no difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just need a level of clarity in terms of what you were relying upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And the only reason is to the extent that you -- you change what was admitted, you are literally changing the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct. That -- and therein lies the rub.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therein lies the rub. Okay. Having settled that, I guess it's my understanding that, Mr. Guy-Smith, you say to the extent you are unhappy with some exhibits, you will get together with your colleague and sort them out?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether what your position is should he be calling those exhibits now before you get an opportunity to sort them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He should not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He doesn't know which they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, we're going to get to them quite rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much. You'll work that out. Where were we? We were at the stage, Mr. Menon, where you -- I need to be reminded, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was seeking the admission of the associated exhibits, and perhaps I can simplify the discussion. The position that we're prepared to take is that we are -- we're willing to live with, obviously, the -- whatever translations exist from the original trial, and that to the extent there are mistakes that need to be corrected -- and I'm talking about really simple mistakes, like the date being incorrectly put on the English translation. To the extent that there are such mistakes, we will simply apply to the Chamber to revise -- to have a revised translation added to e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But we're willing to live with the existing record, because I would like to actually have the associated exhibits admitted at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any problem with that, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may, if I could have but one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I give you a moment. In the meantime we are waiting for Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Emmerson, can Mr. Haradinaj's Defence confirm that, in fact, it has said it doesn't object to the associated --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Harvey -- are you trying to find your microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, I'm trying to find your question, Your Honour. I didn't hear it. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. My question was: Do you have any comment to make on the application by the Prosecution to tender into evidence the associated exhibits that go with the statement of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Do -- is your moment over now, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, my moment is over now. I believe that we can live with that solution subject to, once again, the potential that adds to some -- to the discrete number of exhibits that I'm concerned about, we may have to have them withdrawn or changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- what Mr. Menon is saying is he will live with those mistakes. He's not going to tender in changed translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it will be ...[Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Part of the difficulty here is what has been put into e-court and what we have been given as the translated document is not the same document that we had in the original trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you were going to sort that out with him --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will try to sort that out. So there may come a time when we're going to be changing the documents. By "changing," I mean putting in the originals, the original translations from the first proceeding. Am I clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Okay. That being the case, then the associated exhibits are admitted into evidence, and may they please be given exhibit numbers seriatim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I would read out the 92 ter summary for this witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: With your leave, I would read out the 92 ter summary for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you do that, just to place on record the caveat that Mr. Guy-Smith said, that there may be a need to swap translations, depending on what the situation is that arises. Yes, you may come up with the application -- you leave to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Read out the 92 ter summary for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may do so, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: The witness was formerly a professional soldier in the JNA, the ARBiH, and then the KLA. In March 1998, he went to Tirana in Albania and set about training KLA soldiers in Albania and providing advice on weaponry to KLA members. Around the 28th of May, 1998, the witness crossed the Albania-Kosovo border with approximately 80 armed KLA soldiers. Members of the KLA General Staff were in this group. Following his entry into Kosovo, the witness was tasked with training, inspecting, and advising KLA forces, as well as checking on the KLA forces in the western Kosovo KLA operational zones. In July 1998, the witness was appointed as the director of the operational department of the KLA General Staff. Shortly thereafter, around mid-July 1998, the witness travelled to the Dukagjin zone and toured the zone over a three-day period. The witness describes this tour in his evidence. The witness's first visit during this tour was in the village of Jabllanice in Djakovica municipality, where he and other members of the KLA General Staff met Ramush Haradinaj. The witness also visited units in the village of Jabllanice. During his tour of the Dukagjin area, the witness also visited the village of Gllogjan where Ramush Haradinaj was based and he visited certain neighbouring villages around Gllogjan with Ramush Haradinaj. In late August or early September 1998, the witness and a delegation from the KLA General Staff visited the Dukagjin area again and intervened in a dispute concerning Ramush Haradinaj's leadership over the zone. The KLA General Staff sided with Ramush Haradinaj in this dispute. After being appointed as Chief of Staff of the KLA General Staff in November 1998, the witness personally received reports from Ramush Haradinaj. Having received such reports, the witness had the opportunity to see Haradinaj's signature. The witness was shown a number of Prosecution exhibits and has provided commentary on those documents, including the signature of Ramush Haradinaj which appears on many of those documents. That's the end of my summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Menon. Any cross-examination, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: That was the end of my summary, but I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm running ahead of myself, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could call up document 03011 on e-court. And the witness should be shown the Albanian version, and then the translation and the Albanian should be shown to the rest of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well sir, do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Now, midway down the document - and I think in the Albanian version it's the start of the third paragraph, and in the English version it appears as the start of the second paragraph - there's a sentence which reads: "Voksh is grateful to the KLA special unit led by the Togeri because were it not for this fighter and his hinds, the village of Voksh would today be in the hands of the Serboslav chauvinist enemy ..." Do you see that sentence, sir?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Do you know who the reference to Togeri is? Who is Togeri?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. This report speaks about Togeri, who was the commander of the rapid intervention unit in the Dukagjini zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you know his full real name?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, Idriz Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, based upon your experiences in the Dukagjin zone why -- why this soldier would be writing to Ramush Haradinaj about Togeri?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've -- I've indicated to the witness that based upon his experience -- to answer the question based upon his experience in the Dukagjin zone. And I would note, actually, that the witness -- I mean, in his previous evidence at the time of this particular document he held a senior position within the KLA; that's well established on the record. So there is a sufficient basis for him to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Zyrapi, first of all, has not been qualified as a psychologist nor engaged in the ability to render any expert opinion with regard to the thinking of another person. And there's not a causal connection between the offer of proof made by Mr. Menon and the question asked. It still calls for speculation on its part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do think your question is speculative, Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who Togeri reported to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, that assumes -- it's both leading and it assumes a fact not the in evidence, that Togeri reported to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, before you respond, I would also join that objection. This witness has already testified that he has no idea who appointed the Black Eagles, what their area of operation was, how much independence or autonomy they had. That was his testimony in the previous trial at T 3356, so he's not in a position to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that in the testimony that has just been tendered --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, that was his testimony in the previous trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That has just been tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If I may respond. The witness indicated that the rapid intervention unit in Dukagjin and in the others were under the command of the zone commander and that's also from his initial trial. So there is a basis for me to put the question to the witness. Again, it was -- well -- I mean, the difficulty here is that the foundation exists and it exists in his initial testimony. And what Defence counsel essentially seek for me to do is to go through the entire testimony with this witness because that's what would be required in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, maybe for the sake of this Chamber, which was not in the previous trial, if you can go to that part of the previous testimony that has now been tendered which forms the basis for your question, start there. You don't have to go through the entire evidence, but start where you find the basis and develop from there to get to your question that you want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, did you have -- during your visit to the Dukagjin zone, can you tell us -- can you tell us which villages you visited, sir?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. On the first day, when I arrived, I first visited Jabllanice; on the second day, I visited Gllogjan and some surrounding villages, Irzniq, Prilep, Shaptej. These were the villages I toured on the second day. On the third day, I toured the rest of the territory, Reke e Keqe territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, when you visited the village of Irzniq, can you tell us whether anyone accompanied you on that visit?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. Together with me was the commander of the operational zone, Mr. Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us whether you met any KLA members in the village Irzniq?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. When I visited Irzniq together with the zone commander, we visited the rapid intervention unit where Toger was. I met also Shemsedin Ceku, the commander of the other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, were you -- let me clarify this: When you visited the rapid intervention unit, sir, in Irzniq, can you be precise who you were with?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In the rapid intervention unit I was with the zone commander, Ramush Haradinaj, where the rapid intervention unit was located, in Irzniq.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And was this the first time that you had met with a commander of a rapid intervention unit within the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Very well. And, sir, can you tell us whether you learned at that time who the rapid intervention unit based in -- the -- let me rephrase that, Your Honour. Can you tell us at that time whether you learned who Idriz Balaj reported to as the commander of the rapid intervention unit in Irzniq?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time, the rapid intervention unit reported to the zone commander, Mr. Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And how do you know that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Because of the fact that I was together with the zone commander when I visited the area and the fact that the unit reported to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to have 65 ter 03011 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03011 will be Exhibit P162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can we call up 65 ter 01265. And again, the Albanian should be shown to the witness, and the English and the Albanian version should be shown in the rest of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, there's a reference in this document to Tropoja. Can you tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Tropoja is located in the territory of the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And then there's a reference in the document to a Commander Ramush. Can you tell us who that may be.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This request, this document, refers to Commander Mr. Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us who -- can you tell us whether you know how -- how weapons were transferred to KLA soldiers from the Dukagjin zone through this facility in Tropoja?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Most of the weapons were shipped through mules or horses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But can you tell us, if you know, sir, who was responsible for providing weapons to soldiers who came from the Dukagjin zone to Albania. Who within Albania would be responsible for transferring equipment to those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At the time the person -- the persons responsible for them were the members of the logistical department who were situated in the northern part of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you tell us who those members of the logistics department were?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: At that time that I knew them, they were Xhavit Haliti, Raif Gashi, Xhemal Fetahu, Ilir Konushevci, with whom I had most contacts and co-operated and that I know that they belonged to the logistics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And in what context, sir, did you have contacts and co-operate with these men?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: This was at the time I was in Albania, during which time I co-operated with them. I gave them advice on the technical aspect of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know -- can you tell us in which period these men, the four men that you referred to, in which period they assisted in supplying the Dukagjin zone with weapons?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: During all the time that I was in contact with them, and then, after that, up to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you be a little more specific, sir, and refer to months and years?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I can't be specific about the months, but from April 1998 or May 1998, June, July, and then after that, also in September. Some of them continued to do this job, to work in the logistics department and to supply weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you tell us whom these men would have had contacts with within the leadership of the Dukagjin zone?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The men I mentioned, Xhemal, Faik Gashi, Ilir Konushevci, they had contacts, regular contacts, regarding arms supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But can you tell us whom they would contact in the Dukagjin zone in order to arrange the transport of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: I had no precise information at the time about every single aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, sir. I won't pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 01265 will be Exhibit P163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, with your leave, the next -- I intend to show the witness hard copies of the next seven documents because I think it would be a little more efficient. And if perhaps the Defence would like to inspect the documents before it's shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, with regard to the last document that has been admitted, I have just been informed by Mr. Zyberi, and I'm thankful that he's here because he does speak Albanian, that there are words that are in the English translation that do not appear in the Albanian original. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could we once again, please, have a look at P163. Can you point out the words, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The words are "for ages now," which is the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Those three words, "for ages now" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are not in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are not in the Albanian original, I am told.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, this is -- the translation was the one that was relied upon that was listed for the original Haradinaj trial. So we haven't altered this translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was tendered in the original Haradinaj trial. Well, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this is an example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is an example of one of those places where I think Judge Delvoie's direction becomes important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then, of course, from what we discussed a few moments ago with you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- we can't change it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can't change it. So we do need to make a determination about whether or not the translation, as it stands, is accurate or not for purposes of you, as fact-finders, to give it whatever weight and use whatever way you wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The record now shows that you have told the Chamber that the words "for ages now" are not in the original. So that flags it for us. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry about that, Mr. Menon. You can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I was referring to Exhibits 1266, 1267, 1268, 1269, 3007, 3009 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: -- and 3013. So Your Honours should have copies of that in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I trust that the witness has hard copies as well. Again, for the record, these are the versions of the exhibit that are stored in the evidence unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, I would just ask you to carefully go through each document and to look at the bottom right-hand corner of each document to see if you recognise whose signature it is. And once you've gone through them, if you can tell us whether you recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you go through each document, sir, first. Sir, have you had a chance to go through each document?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the signatures on each document? And I'm talking about the signature on the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you tell us whose signature that is?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI

utterances.text: And can you tell us what type of documents those are?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to have 65 ter exhibits 1266, 1267, 1268, 1269, 3007, 3009, and 3013 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: Microphone for --
