utterances.text: My apologies. I will start all over again. Those documents that were mentioned by counsel from 1266 up to 3013 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar, at your leisure out of court, or do you have --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You already have assigned. Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1266 will be Exhibit P164; 65 ter 1267 will be Exhibit P165; 65 ter 1268 will be Exhibit P166; 65 ter 1269 will be Exhibit P167; 65 ter 3007 will be Exhibit P168; 65 ter 3009 will be Exhibit P169; and 65 ter 3013 will be Exhibit P170. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, if we could call up 65 ter 03048, and, again, the Albanian for the witness and the Albanian and the English for the rest of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, do you the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can I direct you again to the signature at the bottom of the document, in the bottom right-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can you tell us whose signature that is? If you know, sir.

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: Yes. The signature is that of Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask for this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03048 will be Exhibit P171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And before we leave this document, sir, can you tell us in the summer of 1998 when you visited -- in which periods you visited the Dukagjin zone, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: In the summer of 1998, first, I went there in the middle of July; and for the second time, it was end of August or beginning of September. It was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And you see in the document in front of you there's a reference to the author of the document thanking the village of Jabllanice for their constant readiness to help the Kosovo Liberation Army. Sir, do you know, based upon your experiences in the Dukagjin zone in the summer of 1998, what the author of the document is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I mean, it's another speculative question on which is entirely of the same character as the one as Your Honour has already ruled shouldn't be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entirely in your hands. Obviously I've linked it to the witness's visits to the Dukagjin zone. I presume that if the witness is unable to answer the question, then he can tell us that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I raise for another reason which is a document that's dated the 25th of October, which is a considerable period of time after the summer months that have been discussed here, may or may not be a linkage. I don't think that Mr. Menon has linked the document at all. He's made an assumption, he's made an internal assumption as to what's going on, but the evidence has not been given to this Chamber which makes that assumption necessarily one upon which we can get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness's evidence is that he visited in the middle of the July and then it was the end of August or the beginning of September. So it's not such a -- there isn't such a lengthy period between the date of this document and the witness's last visit to the Dukagjin zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That I accept. But nonetheless, it still remains a bit speculative the way it's phrased, that question. It's not for the Bench to tell you how to ask questions, but it is -- the phraseology of the question to which Mr. Emmerson objected was speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to move on. You can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Okay, well, I'll put -- if I can just consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sir, when you visited the Dukagjin zone in the months you've referred to, July and either the end of August or the beginning of September, were you aware of any assistance that the village of Jabllanice provided to Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: It was in general, not only Jabllanice. Many other villages of Kosova, not only Dukagjin zone, offered to help with food or provide their houses at the disposal of the KLA. So it was, in general, an assistance provided to the KLA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- can you be a little more specific as to the assistance that was provided?

utterances.speaker: BISLIM ZYRAPI
utterances.text: The assistance consisted in foodstuffs or in providing their homes to the KLA to accommodate itself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could move on to 65 ter Exhibit 03002, and I'd ask that page 138 be brought up in the English version and page 132 be brought up in the Albanian version. And only the Albanian for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: An objection which goes to conduct as well as substance. The Prosecution are well aware this is an excerpt from the book that objection has been taken to in our opening brief and in the course of Mr. Rogers's opening. Now, you have ordered that any supplemental evidence that this witness is to give should be the subject of notice. We received notice from the Prosecution in the form of a supplemental information sheet relating to a number of documents. This is not one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Menon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, and I'm actually looking for the reference now, but this witness commented on -- on the excerpt which I plan to show him in his November 2005 statement. So the Defence are on notice and it's -- and the document itself is listed on the notification we provided to the witness [sic] as documents to be shown to the witness. So the Defence have notice of the material. There's no prejudice here.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honours ordered that his previous testimony and statements would be admitted to the record as they have been, and to the extent that he has answered questions in relation to this extract, that is already in evidence. Your Honours further ordered that any additional evidence that was sought to be elicited viva voce needed to be the subject of direct notice from the Prosecution. We received direct notice from the Prosecution on the 22nd of August, and for obvious reasons, given that we object to the admissibility of this document, the first thing we looked for was to see whether they were seeking to tender it, and they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: If I can quote from Your Honours' decision, what it says is that: "The Chamber accepts that the Prosecution's submissions that this additional examination-in-chief is based on written statements and transcripts which have been disclosed to the accused." And the November 2005 statement has been in the Defence's possession for a very long time. So that's -- it's entirely fair game. And indeed it's -- the portions of that statement which -- in which the witness commented on this particular extract have been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you. I saw you -- were you rising again, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now -- and you're saying, Mr. Menon, that this page that you have put on the screen is mentioned in the written statements or in the transcripts that are mentioned in that quotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: And I need to find the reference, but the extract which is being shown to the witness is actually commented upon in paragraph -- in paragraph 46 of the statement which the Chamber admitted. It was numbered 65 ter 00118. I don't have the exhibit number which was subsequently assigned. So I can't see how possibly the Defence could claim that they don't have notice or that they're prejudiced by this. This evidence is on the record, and what I'm simply trying to do is have the witness adopt what he previously said so that the extract can go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is this, and I would imagine Mr. Menon must be familiar with this: The portion of this witness's statement that deals with this document was not admitted into evidence by the original Trial Chamber because this document was part of the book that the Trial Chamber excluded. And so for the same reason as in relation to the previous witness, and the relevant passage is paragraph 46 of the witness statement of this witness, the 92 ter statement, the outcome was effectively exactly the same as those passages I took you to at the end of the last witness's evidence, where the Trial Chamber regarded paragraph 46 as unsourced and therefore irrelevant because it had excluded the content document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just add that -- I think Your Honours have made it clear on several occasions that we are not living in the shadow of the last trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, I'm not suggesting we were, but Mr. Menon is seeking to suggest that notice has been given and the matter is properly put before this Trial Chamber by reason of the admission of the 92 ter. It is no more before this Trial Chamber than those, if you like, empty vacuum vessel passages in the statement of the previous witness, where it purported to exhibit something which was not then exhibited. What Mr. Menon is, in fact, doing is inviting this Trial Chamber to admit this document for the first time, which is, in fact, in substance what he is doing that is objected to, and no notice has been given in relation to it. They know it's objected to. The issue hasn't been argued. Your Honours prevented Mr. Rogers, quite rightly, from opening it. There is no question of this passage having been admitting it. The Trial Chamber excluded it. It, therefore, is not part of the 92 ter. The relevant paragraph is vacuous and empty of content and unsourced. And what Mr. Menon is trying to do is to circumvent the requirement to give notice and have a ruling on the admissibility of this book. In order to get the book admitted, as I indicated to Your Honour at the outset and as is indicated in our opening brief, it would be necessary for the Prosecution to be in a position to prove the provenance of the book, the authorship, the methodology and its reliability. They haven't done that. They haven't sought to do it. And seeking, so to speak, through this witness -- it has nothing to do with the production of this book, and there is nothing about the way in which it was produced to append a single page from it which is not, in fact, in evidence. So to the extent that the 92 ter statement is, the document is not and neither is the relevant passage. It's a simple technique to subvert the basic procedure that has been agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just add, Mr. Emmerson brought up the issue of notice, and, as I mentioned previously, there is no issue of notice. If the extract was in -- the material from the statement is obviously in the statement. It's been admitted, so there's no issue as to what the witness previously said. The document itself, the book, is among the exhibits that we notified the Defence that we intended to show to the witness. And as far as what the last Trial Chamber decided as to the admissibility of this exhibit, it's simply not relevant as Your Honours have indicated. It may be -- there may be some persuasive authority, but it's not binding on this particular Court. And what I intend to do is to show the witness an extract where his name is referenced, he's referred to in the document, and simply to have him read the document and ask whether it's accurate. Obviously if he's referred to in the document then he should be in a position to confirm its accuracy or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem we find ourselves in is that if -- if Mr. Emmerson is right, this Chamber has given an order prohibiting the Prosecution from tendering the book which includes this page, pending further issues to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't recall that such an order was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's why I say if he's right --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't recall myself, and I'm rely entirely on counsel to remind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Secondly, I'm not seeking to tender seeking the whole book. What I would be tendering is the extract on which the witness comments, not the whole book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, except that the page is part of a document that is being objected against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But I don't see the problem. If the witness is capable of commenting on the book, which he should be, given the fact that he's referred to in the context of a meeting -- and I'm beginning to testify, so I'm going to stop. But surely he should be able to comment on that. He should be able to tell us whether it's accurate or not and based upon that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, he is beginning to testify --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It's a little difficult given the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He hasn't told us what's in the book. He hasn't told us the contents of the so he hasn't begun to testify. He is just saying he could tell us whether it's accurate or not accurate, whatever is being said about him in the book. He hasn't begun to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now just for my clarification, this extract of the book, after having put it to the witness, your intention is to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it is not on the 92 ter document list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It was not included -- perhaps it could have been included as among the associated exhibits but it wasn't. So that's why it was included among the list of exhibits that we intended to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And that has been notified to the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But Mr. Emmerson says he doesn't have notice of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I don't think that Mr. Emmerson is suggesting that he didn't receive the list because they very well did receive the list. And we can produce the e-mail, if necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Would you like me to explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, you did explain. I did understand what you said. You said you haven't gotten notice of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The position is, putting it briefly, the Prosecution indicated in advance of the trial that there are certain documents they might seek to rely upon. This particular passage was never admitted by the Trial Chamber in the previous trial, and, therefore, insofar as they thought it was appended to the 92 ter, it is not. And the relevant passage of the 92 ter is empty of content. Now, an objection was notified to the Prosecution in advance of this trial and again in our opening brief that the whole of the document is objected to because of an absence of proof as to its provenance. At the beginning of this trial, when Mr. Rogers sought to open it, I objected, and I'll give Your Honours the page, it's page 225, line 20, and Your Honour, Judge Moloto, ruled as follows: "Let me just make a general comment. I find the opening to verge on testifying and introducing exhibits which are not marked as exhibits yet but which are documents that make an impression in the mind of the Chamber. And to the extent that at this point there is now a dispute about the authenticity and the provenance, the relevance of the book that you are about to refer to, the Chamber feels constrained to apply the rules of admissibility before it allows you to continue talking about that. You've got to authenticate it. You've got to bring in a witness to say he's the author of the book, all the requirements of admissibility." That hasn't been done. This witness can't authenticate it. It's not currently in evidence. It's improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may correct Mr. Emmerson's recital of the law, I don't think authorship -- as my understanding of the law at this Tribunal, and I don't have the reference in front of me but I can obtain -- is that there is a Celebici Appeals Chamber decision which says that authorship is not a prerequisite to admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He was merely quoting what I said. He was not saying he was postulating what the law says in this Tribunal and if -- and I'm quite prepared to accept that I may not know the law and I should be guided by the parties. Be that as it may, that order then does stand, and it's got to be rescinded before we can [Overlapping speakers]... contrary to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, our understanding is that there is no order prohibiting the Prosecution from presenting a document to a witness, otherwise it becomes very difficult to tender these documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, it's not these documents. It's part of a document that has been objected to and that a Chamber has made an order about. If anything is being said about this witness which you want to check with him whether it's correct or not, you can put it to him what is said to him -- what is said about him and without necessarily using a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- you say is just one -- that part only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our understanding is that there is no such order. The Chamber has not issued an order prohibiting us from showing the document to witnesses who may be able to comment on the document. That's my understanding of the outcome during -- of the opening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can -- I have -- I have a citation from the -- what I believe is the opening that may be helpful. And this is Your Honour speaking -- speaking to Mr. Rogers saying: "I remind you the last" -- and this is in relation to the book. "I remind you the last comment I wanted to make. I think it is important, therefore, where there is a dispute --" THE COURT REPORTER: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Sorry. "Where there is a dispute between the parties about the admissibility of a document, that it be admitted in the normal course. I do not agree with you that the Chamber can read the document to determine its admissibility. Admissibility is determined before the document --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading documents. We're not machines. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: I apologise to the court reporters and the interprets. "Admissibility is determined before the document is tendered. So obviously the normal rules apply. There is no order here, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Can I finish. We can -- this is a document that's on our exhibit list that was notified to the Defence well in advance of this witness's testimony. We can put the document to the witness and ask him to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the dispute because they say that this document is not given to them, it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: It was -- Your Honour, if necessary, I'll need a moment but I can produce the notification. I can produce the e-mail. There's no issue as to the Defence not having been notified that we intended to use this particular exhibit with this particular witness. That cannot be an issue because I'm absolutely certain that on the 20th of August, that that was the last time we sent out a notification that this document was included on that list --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would be grateful if there could be a break between interventions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Interpreter. Now, if I understood Mr. Emmerson well, he says the Prosecution has not given notice of this page. Now, you say there can never be a dispute about that because we've got an e-mail. Obviously you're privy to that, we're not. He is privy to what he is saying. All I can say is there is a dispute, and, therefore, you're going to have to produce proof that you've served it on them, and then at least we can go past the problem of whether or not they had notice of it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just to make sure we're not talking at cross-purposes, I thought I made it clear. The Prosecution notified us that they wished to raise this document with this witness. The position as far as the 92 ter statement is concerned is that it was excluded by the Trial Chamber and therefore the relevant passage of the 92 ter statement is currently without content. For them to be able to raise this document with this witness, they need to prove its provenance. This witness cannot prove its provenance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, wait a minute, Mr. -- wait a minute. I think you are talking about two different things here. You're saying the position, as far as the 92 ter statement is concerned, is that it was excluded by the Trial Chamber, and, therefore, the relevant pages of the 92 ter statement is currently without content. Which relevant parts of the 92 ter statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- were excluded by this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I stand back for a moment and just explain the position overall. The document, as a whole, was not admitted at the previous trial, the first point, the book, including this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Secondly, as a consequence, the 92 ter statement admitted at the previous trial left the paragraph commenting on this book empty of content because it was unsourced. It sought to refer to this paragraph in the book and to make certain comments on it. Obviously, the Trial Chamber in the previous trial, therefore, regarded that paragraph as empty of content because it was unsourced in the same way as the passages of the last witness's testimony that purported to produce and comment on exhibits that were excluded. That, therefore, is the position in relation to the 92 ter statement. It is the same 92 ter statement which Your Honours have just admitted. Therefore, this document has not the yet been admitted either in the previous trial as an -- as an appendix to the 92 ter or in this trial because no application in this trial has been made to admit it. It's quite correct that in August the Prosecution indicated that they wished to do that. They then gave us notification two days ago of what it was they were seeking to produce by way of additional documentation. It doesn't come on that list. In other words, they need -- please sit down for a moment and let me finish. They need to make an application to Your Honours to admit this document. It isn't one of the documents that they gave us notice they were seeking to admit as an additional document. They obviously clearly didn't realise or haven't take on board the fact that it is not yet in evidence. That being the case, they must now, as Your Honour has indicated and indicated right at the outset, establish provenance. Whether authorship is a requirement to establish provenance or not may be a subject for debate. But what is undoubtedly the case is that the Trial Chamber would need to be satisfied about all matters relevant to authenticity, reliability, and probative value. This witness, all he can do is say: As far as I am concerned, X, Y, and Z are factually the position. And then if the Prosecution subsequently applies to have the book admitted they can say: Well, one of the things that goes to that is that X, Y, and Z are said in that passage of the book. And then, therefore, at least in that passage, there is an objective corroborative evidence from this witness confirming what that passage says. That's not the same as allowing this witness to prove provenance of a book or even a passage of a book that he's not in a position to comment about either the production or the manufacture of. So what Mr. Menon cannot do -- given that this passage has never been admitted and that there is a currently existing objection to it, whether or not he's notified us that he'd like to, what he cannot do is to use this witness to prove the provenance of a book he had nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just correct one thing. The notification that was provided to the Defence a couple of days ago was a supplemental information sheet. What that contained was additional information or corrections that this witness had indicated to us during the proofing session. That was not meant to override the earlier notification that had been sent to the Defence on the 20th of August, notifying them that this book was among the exhibits that we intended to show to the witness. And I think the Defence know that, and I think that is a bit of a misrepresentation. And I go back to the Chamber decision on 92 ter where it indicated that the subject of additional examination-in-chief is based on written statements and transcripts which have been disclosed to the accused, and that -- we satisfied that, so there can be no issue here -- let me finish. Mr. Emmerson keeps drawing it back to the initial trial and the initial Trial Chamber's decision to exclude that exhibit. With respect, Your Honour, once again, as Your Honours have aptly noted, this Trial Chamber is not living in the shadow of the prior Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, whether or not this Trial Chamber is living or not living in the shadow of the former trial which now is going to become refrained every time the Prosecution wishes to do something, is irrelevant. What is relevant is that this Trial Chamber made an order. That order was that this matter was in dispute and provenance had to be proved. Whether or not you are correct or incorrect on the law, as has been suggested by Mr. Menon and Mr. Rogers, once again, is also irrelevant. And I'll give you a perfect example of that because we had it happen earlier today. Mr. Emmerson stood and began to use a document, and there was objection taken to that document as a result of it not being in conformity with this Trial Chamber's order. And you said, and rightfully so: You need to make an application, sir, before you attempt to use that document. At which point Mr. Emmerson did that. There is nothing different there with regard to the issue of your order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's really fundamental. An order was made and now they're trying to get around the order that was made by saying you're wrong on the law, or there is an issue with regard to notice. Those are smoke-screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MENON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. We are all jumping around and talking all at the same time now. I have been notified we are well beyond our time and that we must get out of court. You will have to argue this point tomorrow. And I would like the parties to please bring in the various orders that they've been referring to in hard copy. We're taking an adjournment.
